newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Forgers beware -- HK passport photos self-destruct.
newsitem.headline: Forgers beware -- HK passport photos self-destruct.

text.p: Hong Kong is taking no chances -- its new passport will have a high-tech image of the traveller that will "self-destruct" if tampered with, "just like in Mission Impossible".
That's how immigration chief Regina Ip described the top-security document when she flashed it to the media on Friday.

With just 25 days to go until the bustling territory ends its 156 years as a British colony and starts life as a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China, the passport is essential for many Hong Kong people wanting to travel abroad after July 1.
Virtually science-fiction security features "will make the passport very difficult to forge", Ip told reporters.
Instead of a photo, the passports will hold a "digitised" image of the holder printed on a laminate surface "which will self-destruct if tampered with, just like in Mission Impossible", Ip said.

Other measures include special printing techniques, information that shows up only under ultraviolet light and two photo codes that reproduce the traveller's image when passed under a reader, she said.

Many countries have waited until the last minute to recognise the document, fearing it might be insecure and fall into the hands of mainland Chinese emigrants who could abuse it to enter foreign countries illegally.

Recently, however, Britain, the United States, Canada, Australia, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines, Turkey and seven other countries have recognised the SAR passport and announced favourable conditions of entry ranging from easy visas to visa-free access.
The European Union is poised to follow suit soon.
The SAR passport, which sports a deep blue cover with gold lettering and the five-star seal of the People's Republic of China, will be issued starting in early July, Ip said.

People in Hong Kong can pick up application forms at immigration offices and post offices from June 10, while Hong Kong residents overseas will be able to get the forms through 200 Chinese embassies and consulates worldwide in two weeks.

About three million of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people hold some type of British travel document such as the British National Overseas passport, which grants no residency rights in Britain but confers some consular protection and travel convenience.

The rest of the territory's people hold only a local travel document that confers no nationality. A number of residents -- estimated at up to 750,000 -- hold full passports from countries such as Canada, Australia, the United States and Britain.
About 5.5 million Hong Kong residents will be eligible to apply for the new SAR passports, Ip said.
China has pledged strict procedures to prevent mainland immigrants from pouring into Hong Kong after the handover.
"Both legal and illegal immigration from China is under control," Ip said, adding that the territory's immigration procedures would not change after July 1.
Every day, about 150 mainland residents come to Hong Kong legally, while another 50 are caught after sneaking across the border, she said.
